article_title: Commentary on Interest-Driven Creator theory: a US perspective on fostering interest, creativity, and habit in school
citation: Roschelle, J., & Burke, Q. (2019). Commentary on Interest-Driven Creator theory: a US perspective on fostering interest, creativity, and habit in school. Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning, 14(13). https://doi.org/10.1186/s41039-019-0107-2
title: Schools should both celebrate student creations and regularly cultivate creativity
description: The commentary proposes that schools need both a focus on creation (students' novel, expressive artifacts showcased in classrooms and corridors) and a focus on creativity (regular space in assignments for creative response). The authors hypothesize the two reinforce each other: celebrating creations breathes energy into the habit of creativity, while regular cultivation leads to more authentic and meaningful creations.
requirements: Schools must create space in assignments for students to respond creatively and nurture creativity regularly, not only in showpiece production
target_learning_goals: Creativity
Sustained creative habits
examples: The authors describe progressive US schools displaying student artifacts on shelves, walls, display cases, and district offices while teachers articulate how they nurture creativity regularly
key_sources: Roschelle, J., & Burke, Q. (2019). Commentary on Interest-Driven Creator theory: a US perspective on fostering interest, creativity, and habit in school. Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning, 14(13). https://doi.org/10.1186/s41039-019-0107-2

article_title: Practitioners at the Center, Part II: Reflections on Practitioners’ Engagement with the SEERNet Hub
citation: Pautz Stephenson, S., & Pakhira, D. (2023). Practitioners at the Center, Part II: Reflections on Practitioners' Engagement with the SEERNet Hub. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/196
title: Center practitioners in education research by including diverse expertise, shifting power in research question design, and engaging them in feedback loops from design to dissemination
description: Digital Promise's six guiding principles for practitioner engagement in SEERNet hold that researchers should include practitioners with diverse backgrounds and expertise, empower practitioners and shift power dynamics especially in creating research questions, value their lived experiences as content and context experts, surface problems of practice, structure feedback loops, and disseminate findings so platforms are used widely and well. The report urges researchers to "see the value of practitioners' lived experiences and engage them in feedback loops from design to implementation to dissemination."
requirements: Existing formal or informal networks to support recruitment of a diverse group of participants
Feedback loops that are purposeful, bidirectional, and iterative
constraints: DLP research can be technically completed with limited to no interaction with practitioners, making deliberate engagement choices necessary
target_learners: K-12 and higher education practitioners, including educators serving historically and systematically excluded communities
target_learning_goals: Research questions and study designs that address problems of practice and improve equity in research and learning
examples: Office Hours used pre-readings, stated norms, Jamboard activities, and 1:1 meetings to ensure practitioner voices were heard; the advisory board was compensated for sustained engagement
key_sources: Pautz Stephenson, S., & Pakhira, D. (2023). Practitioners at the Center, Part II: Reflections on Practitioners' Engagement with the SEERNet Hub. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/196

article_title: The Center of Black Student Excellence: A Place without Barriers and the 10 Elements That Lay Its Foundation
citation: Powell, K. (2024). The center of black student excellence: A place without barriers and the 10 elements that lay its foundation. Long Beach Unified School District. https://www.wested.org
title: The Center of Black Student Excellence (CBSE)
description: The CBSE is a planned district entity in LBUSD described as "a visionary establishment whose design is shaped by and for the Black Community where they can proudly discover and honor their identity, history, and cultural heritage, which fosters a sense of inclusion and confidence." It is more than a physical location: a commitment to nurturing belonging, pride, and agency among Black students and families. The Center will offer tutoring, mentoring, cultural programming, wellness services, legal aid, career support, and advocacy, and will act as a bridge between the district and the Black Community.
requirements: Ongoing dialogue and input with the Black Community to refine its design and programmatic offerings
constraints: The Center is not tasked with reversing harm done to Black students and families; that responsibility lies with the school system, per the brief
target_learning_goals: Identity, belonging, agency, academic and life outcomes
examples: The brief states the Center will assist schools in examining ways to effectively integrate the 10 Elements of Black Excellence in programs and classrooms
key_sources: Powell, K. (2024). The center of black student excellence: A place without barriers and the 10 elements that lay its foundation. Long Beach Unified School District. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED663856

article_title: Navigating a Sea of Reforms: Sustaining School Health Centers through Statewide Initiatives
citation: Eisenberg, L., Sabalburo, E., & Ford, J. (2025). Navigating a sea of reforms: Sustaining school health centers through statewide initiatives. Alameda County Health, Healthy Schools and Communities. https://WestEd.org
title: Certified Wellness Coach provider type
description: Certified Wellness Coach is "a newly defined provider type designed to increase the capacity of schools and community-based partners to support the behavioral health needs of youth." Coaches deliver nonclinical services—wellness promotion and education, screening, care coordination, individual and group support, and crisis referral—under supervision of Pupil Personnel Services credentialed holders or licensed clinicians. A state certification program launched in January 2024 with education and workforce pathways; SHC managers saw the role as aligned with existing unlicensed staff such as case managers and health educators.
requirements: Positions work as part of a larger care team under supervision of Pupil Personnel Services credentialed holders or licensed clinicians
Workforce-pathway applicants need an associate or bachelor's degree and at least 1,350 hours of related experience
constraints: Certified Wellness Coaches are not eligible providers in current FQHC prospective payment system rates, creating a disincentive for FQHC-sponsored SHCs to hire them
SHCs are reluctant to add positions without a clear picture of long-term sustainability through Fee Schedule billing
target_learners: Students and youth up to age 24 in Alameda County public schools
target_learning_goals: Behavioral health and well-being support for youth, including wellness promotion, screening, and care coordination
examples: SHCs identified schoolwide prevention activities, classroom presentations, care coordination, and case management as services fitting the wellness coach role
key_sources: Eisenberg, L., Sabalburo, E., & Ford, J. (2025). Navigating a sea of reforms: Sustaining school health centers through statewide initiatives. Alameda County Health, Healthy Schools and Communities. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673564

article_title: Community Schools Certification: An Approach for Implementation
citation: Germain, E., Maier, A., Espinoza, D., & Oakes, J. (2025). Community schools certification: An approach for implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/220.412
title: Design certification processes to focus on continuous improvement rather than compliance and accountability
description: The report finds certification processes offer the most value when organized around continuous improvement rather than compliance. Promising strategies include "offering general and targeted technical assistance; creating peer and mentor networks for community schools coordinators; having an assigned coach; building in check-ins and feedback sessions, including peer reviewers in the certification process; and maintaining a resource library for participants." Establishing phases or tiers with clearly defined thresholds lets schools achieve baseline implementation, celebrate growth, and strive for excellence, keeping certification formative rather than punitive.
requirements: The certifying entity must invest sufficient resources to support onboarding and ongoing coaching of district and school personnel, staff the evaluation process, and expand as more schools apply.
constraints: The tension between formative support and compliance orientation remains; the amount of time allotted for schools to attain certification should be long enough to engage meaningfully and deepen implementation year over year.
target_learning_goals: effective implementation of the community schools strategy
continuous improvement
examples: All three certification systems examined were designed to center on continuous improvement.
key_sources: Germain, E., Maier, A., Espinoza, D., & Oakes, J. (2025). Community schools certification: An approach for implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/220.412

article_title: Sustaining AI-enabled student support: A four-year implementation and impact study
citation: Mata, Catherine, Emily Russell, and Lindsay C. Page. (2026). Sustaining AI-Enabled Student Support: A Four-Year Implementation and Impact Study. (EdWorkingPaper: 26-1409). Annenberg Institute at Brown University. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai26-1409
title: Sustaining chatbot-based student communication requires centralized institutional ownership and flexibility in communication strategy
description: The article concludes that a centrally operated chatbot, housed in a designated administrative home, is essential for sustaining communication goals and coordinating the data flows across university offices needed for effective outreach. It also finds that "a certain level of flexibility within the overarching communication strategy is crucial," allowing administrators to adapt to evolving student needs, new cohorts, and external shocks such as the COVID-19 pandemic. The principle generalizes the authors' implementation lessons to other institutions deploying communication technologies.
requirements: A central office or chatbot team that owns campaign design and distribution
Cross-unit coordination and data sharing for tailored outreach
constraints: The siloed nature of data and recordkeeping at CSUN made targeted campaigns burdensome and difficult to sustain over time
target_learners: Undergraduate students at large urban public universities
target_learning_goals: Navigation of financial, logistical, and administrative tasks required for continued enrollment
Sense of belonging and social connectedness on campus
examples: CSUN jointly oversaw its chatbot through the Office of Undergraduate Studies and the Office of the Registrar, with a designated communication specialist crafting all campaigns for consistency of voice
key_sources: Mata, Catherine, Emily Russell, and Lindsay C. Page. (2026). Sustaining AI-Enabled Student Support: A Four-Year Implementation and Impact Study. (EdWorkingPaper: 26-1409). Annenberg Institute at Brown University. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai26-1409

article_title: Design and Implementation of a Real-time Multi-site Immersive Learning System Using Photon Fusion
citation: Iwai Wataru, Duc V . Nguyen. (2026). Design and Implementation of a Real-Time Multi-Site Immersive Learning System Using Photon Fusion. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10325
title: Central-server synchronization pattern replacing peer-to-peer HMD relaying for multi-user VR classrooms
description: The design pattern routes all client communication through Photon Cloud as a central server that synchronizes object states and audio among all clients in real time, instead of the prior peer-to-peer arrangement whose performance "depended on the processing power of the Head-Mounted Display (HMD)". This decouples stability from individual headset processing load and supports simultaneous multi-user participation.
requirements: A central synchronization server (Photon Cloud) reachable by all clients over Wi-Fi
constraints: The prior peer-to-peer approach became unstable with multiple users, with FPS unstable and only up to five participants possible
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in VR-supported lessons
target_learning_goals: real-time shared manipulation of 3D learning materials with voice communication
examples: The proposed system integrates Photon Fusion with Photon Voice 2 so that voice communication is initiated in conjunction with the client's entry into the VR classroom
key_sources: Lb0

article_title: Aligning ChatGPT with E-Portfolio Assessment as EFL Learning Model: Its Effect on Students' Speaking Performance and Feedback Literacy
citation: I Putu Yoga Laksana, Ni Made Ratminingsih, Made Hery Santosa & I Putu Indra Kusuma. (2026). Aligning ChatGPT with E-Portfolio Assessment as EFL Learning Model: Its Effect on Student's Speaking Performance and Feedback Literacy. Technology in Language Teaching & Learning, 8, 103616. https://doi.org/10.29140/tltl.2026.103616
title: The CEA model: ChatGPT aligned with e-portfolio assessment as an integrated EFL learning framework
description: The CEA model integrates ChatGPT with e-portfolio assessment so that AI-generated individualized feedback and portfolio-based documentation, peer feedback, and reflection operate as one learning ecosystem. In the study, "Padlet as the primary e-portfolio environment and ChatGPT as the individualized feedback system represented the entire practical framework of the CEA model." Students practiced speaking with ChatGPT voice-mode interaction, recorded video performances, uploaded them to Padlet, exchanged peer comments, and wrote self-reflections via Google Form. The model is grounded in social cognitive, constructivist, and connectivist theories and was designed to cultivate critical assessment of AI feedback, since AI feedback cannot be assumed universally reliable.
requirements: Structured pedagogical integration: students must be taught how to interact with ChatGPT (e.g., voice-mode interaction) and to use the e-portfolio for feedback, reflection, and archiving, rather than having unrestricted access
constraints: The control condition in the study was traditional e-portfolio practice without structured AI integration, not a completely AI-free group; the researchers could not rule out independent out-of-class AI access
The authors identify the differing affordances of Padlet versus Google Drive as a possible confounding variable
target_learning_goals: EFL speaking performance (fluency, accuracy, complexity)
feedback literacy
examples: Over 8 weeks, experimental-group students drafted ideas and practiced with friends and ChatGPT, recorded 3 to 5-minute video performances, uploaded them to Padlet, received lecturer and peer comments, and wrote self-reflections on a Google Form
key_sources: I Putu Yoga Laksana, Ni Made Ratminingsih, Made Hery Santosa & I Putu Indra Kusuma. (2026). Aligning ChatGPT with E-Portfolio Assessment as EFL Learning Model: Its Effect on Student's Speaking Performance and Feedback Literacy. Technology in Language Teaching & Learning, 8, 103616. https://doi.org/10.29140/tltl.2026.103616

article_title: Developmental Dyslexia and Dysgraphia: What can We Learn from the One About the Other?
citation: Döhla D and Heim S (2016). Developmental Dyslexia and Dysgraphia: What can We Learn from the One About the Other? Front. Psychol. 6:2045. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.02045
title: Cerebellar deficit hypothesis: impaired cerebellar automatization causes reading, writing and spelling problems via distinct routes
description: The review describes the cerebellar deficit hypothesis (Nicolson et al., 2001; Nicolson and Fawcett, 2011), in which the cerebellum supports automatization of articulatory, auditory and motor skills. "a dysfunctional cerebellum can lead to reading as well as writing disorders": writing problems arise from motor skill difficulties, reading problems from phonology based on deficient articulatory skills, and spelling problems from deficient skill automatization, with different cerebellar regions activated for each route. Nicolson and Fawcett's three-stage automaticity-deficit framework (declarative, intermediate, autonomous) and five stages of learning are included.
requirements: The framework assumes the cerebellum supports automatization of basic articulatory, auditory and motor skills
constraints: The review reports mixed outcomes: some studies found no significantly worse automatization results between dyslexics and controls
target_learning_goals: automatization of reading, spelling and writing skills
examples: Nicolson and Fawcett (2000) found in a response-blending study that dyslexic children have problems in the initial stage and take longer for intermediate proceduralization
key_sources: Döhla D and Heim S (2016). Developmental Dyslexia and Dysgraphia: What can We Learn from the One About the Other? Front. Psychol. 6:2045. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.02045

article_title: Capturing the participation and social dimensions of computer-supported collaborative learning through social network analysis: which method and measures matter?
citation: Mohammed Saqr, et al. (2020). Capturing the participation and social dimensions of computer-supported collaborative learning through social network analysis: which method and measures matter? International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 15:227–248. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09322-6
title: Centrality measures as operationalization of the participatory and social dimensions of CSCL
description: The article organizes SNA-based CSCL measurement around two dimensions. The participatory dimension is captured by degree centralities: outdegree is "frequently calculated as the number of out-posts generated by a learner" and indicates quantity of participation, while indegree counts replies received and indicates prestige or worthiness of contribution. The social dimension is captured by closeness, betweenness and eigenvector centralities; the article states that "Eigenvector centrality captures the social positioning of the students more reliably than the other centrality measures" because it weighs the centrality of a learner's contacts. The study validates which configurations best measure each dimension.
requirements: A network must be constructed from forum interaction data with an explicit tie definition, direction, weight and aggregation choice
Group-size differences require deciding between normalized and raw centrality versions
constraints: Findings derive from problem-based learning courses in medical higher education using Moodle forums
target_learners: university students in problem-based learning courses
target_learning_goals: measuring participatory effort and social positioning in collaborative knowledge construction
examples: The study computed outdegree, indegree, closeness, betweenness and eigenvector centralities for 598 students across 12 PBL courses in multigraph, simplified and weighted configurations
key_sources: Mohammed Saqr, et al. (2020). Capturing the participation and social dimensions of computer-supported collaborative learning through social network analysis: which method and measures matter? International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 15:227–248. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09322-6

article_title: The modality effect reverses in a virtual reality learning environment and influences cognitive load
citation: Patrick Albus, Tina Seufert. (2023). The modality effect reverses in a virtual reality learning environment and influences cognitive load. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09611-7
title: cellVIEW VR immersive learning unit on HIV
description: An immersive VR learning environment built on the tool cellVIEW for this study, presenting a guided tour through an HIV cell in 3D. Macromolecular structures "only became visible when the learner moved towards or into a component of the virus", and learners could move freely and observe structures from all sides. Verbal explanatory texts were presented either as integrated visual text whose rotation dynamically adapted to the learner's position, or auditorily via headset, with identical wording across conditions. The learning phase lasted on average 11 minutes and was self-paced, with no replay possible.
requirements: Head-mounted display with roomscale tracking and controllers
Text integrated into the VRLE and dynamically rotated for readability
constraints: Replaying content or returning to previous content was not possible
target_learning_goals: macromolecular biology: HIV structure and processes within the virus
examples: Used with a Vive Pro HMD in a between-subjects experiment comparing visual-only and audio-visual text modality
key_sources: Patrick Albus, Tina Seufert. (2023). The modality effect reverses in a virtual reality learning environment and influences cognitive load. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09611-7

article_title: Graphical means for inspecting qualitative models of system behaviour
citation: Anders Bouwer, Bert Bredeweg. (2010). Graphical means for inspecting qualitative models of system behaviour. Instr Sci 38:173–208. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9083-4
title: Cerrado Succession Hypothesis (CSH) qualitative model library for Brazilian Cerrado ecology
description: The CSH model is a GARP model library for the Brazilian Cerrado ecosystem, whose goal is "to provide insight in the causal mechanisms involved in the development and management of the Cerrado ecosystem". "The library for the Cerrado domain contains 79 model fragments", covering description views (population concepts), assumptions (open/closed populations, immigration flows), process fragments (natality, mortality, emigration, immigration, colonization), agent fragments (fire management), and composition views for interactions and vegetational states. Scenarios range from single-population cases to the full three-population succession simulation.
requirements: The GARP simulation engine and a scenario describing initial structure and values
constraints: Scenarios were sequenced from simple to complex, which the authors regard as a curriculum of Cerrado ecology knowledge
target_learners: future decision makers in sustainable development
target_learning_goals: explaining vegetation succession and population dynamics in the Cerrado
understanding causal effects of fire management
examples: The evaluation used two scenarios: a simple one-population scenario (8 states, 8 quantities, 12 dependencies) and a complex Cerrado Succession Hypothesis scenario (19 states, 32 quantities, 127 dependencies)
key_sources: Anders Bouwer, Bert Bredeweg. (2010). Graphical means for inspecting qualitative models of system behaviour. Instr Sci 38:173–208. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9083-4

article_title: Communications and discussions: The doctrine of formal discipline: two neglected instances of transfer of training.
citation: J. E. Wallace Wallin. (1905). The Doctrine of Formal Discipline: Two Neglected Instances of Transfer of Training. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Central (cortical) account of cross-education: practice effects establish cortical tendencies and mental attitudes that generalize
description: The article proposes that transfer of practice between organs is explicable on the assumption that "the effects of practice are central: the training of the one eye established certain cortical tendencies and mental attitudes," so the unused retina responds in harmony with the central predisposition. It allows that peripheral elements, such as sympathetic fixation of the two eyes functioning as a unity, could be involved conjointly. The account is offered as an explanation of the cross-education observed in the reversible-perspective experiments.
requirements: Practice must establish a general disposition or tendency strong enough that an organ not directly exercised shares in it
constraints: The author states the explanation is an assumption and that a tendency of training to spread or generalize holds "whatever the explanation"
target_learners: adult experimental subjects practicing perceptual control tasks
target_learning_goals: perceptual control of reversible perspective figures
transfer of trained perceptual dispositions to unpracticed organs
examples: The author's reversible-perspective series, in which monocular practice transferred to the covered eye, which "acquired by cross-induction a favorable fixation set."
key_sources: J. E. Wallace Wallin. (1905). The Doctrine of Formal Discipline: Two Neglected Instances of Transfer of Training. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org

article_title: A study of superior children.
citation: Sandiford, P., & R. P. (1922). New Publications: reviews of Baldwin's mental growth study, Root's A Socio-Psychological Study of 53 Supernormal Children, and Ballard's Group Tests of Intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Root's central common factor theory of superior intelligence, in which the common factor may be environmental as well as innate
description: The review describes Root's explanatory framework for his results: a central common factor theory in which the common factor underlying superior performance "could just as well be environmental as innate." Root states the factor "may be a varying admixture of innate ability, formal training, incidental education and social conditions." The reviewer reports that Root stresses environmental factors throughout the thesis more than most psychologists would, and the reviewer questions some of these opinions.
requirements: The theory is offered as Root's explanation of his own test and case-history results with superior children, per the review.
constraints: The reviewer reports the conclusions and opinions of the author are open to much debate.
target_learning_goals: explaining the basis of superior intelligence and test performance
examples: Root's monograph presents sociological and psychological study of a small group of superior-IQ children with extensive case histories.
key_sources: Sandiford, P., & R. P. (1922). New Publications: reviews of Baldwin's mental growth study, Root's A Socio-Psychological Study of 53 Supernormal Children, and Ballard's Group Tests of Intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu

article_title: Is plasticity of synapses the mechanism of long-term memory storage?
citation: Wickliffe C. Abraham, Owen D. Jones and David L. Glanzman. (2019). Is plasticity of synapses the mechanism of long-term memory storage? npj Science of Learning 4:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0048-y
title: Cell-intrinsic memory storage via stable epigenetic marks, particularly DNA methylation, is proposed as an alternative to storage in altered synaptic weights
description: This model holds that long-term memories are stored within neuronal nuclei as thermodynamically stable epigenetic changes, chiefly DNA methylation, first proposed by Holliday. The review reports that DNMT inhibitors block memory formation or consolidation and can disrupt well-consolidated memory, that methylation patterns change over weeks after training, and that active demethylation by Tet enzymes means cytosines could in principle subserve a binary code. Synaptic changes would then be the mechanism by which stored nuclear memories are expressed.
requirements: Requires an explanation of how epigenetic changes can faithfully maintain a record of learning-induced changes across the thousands of synaptic connections a neuron maintains; no such explanation is presently at hand
constraints: The synapse specificity problem is the strongest argument against this hypothesis: it appears far more difficult to encode which specific synapses were strengthened in a cell-intrinsic model
target_learners: mammals and invertebrates studied in memory research
target_learning_goals: long-term memory storage, consolidation, and maintenance
examples: Holliday proposed that methylated or non-methylated DNA sites switch a neuron's phenotype so it responds to a previously received signal
key_sources: Wickliffe C. Abraham, Owen D. Jones and David L. Glanzman. (2019). Is plasticity of synapses the mechanism of long-term memory storage? npj Science of Learning 4:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0048-y

article_title: In Search of a More Effective Strategy: Using the 5E Instructional Strategy to Teach Civic Education in Senior Secondary Schools in Ilorin, Nigeria
citation: AbdulRaheem, Y., Bello, M. B., & Odutayo, A. O. (2018). In Search of a More Effective Strategy: Using the 5E Instructional Strategy to Teach Civic Education in Senior Secondary Schools in Ilorin, Nigeria. Journal of International Social Studies, 8(1), 62-85. http://www.iajiss.org
title: Civic Education Literacy Test (CELT), a 50-item multiple-choice instrument
description: The Civic Education Literacy Test (CELT) is the 50-item multiple-choice objective instrument used to collect literacy-score data in this study. Its reliability was measured by split-half with the Spearman-Brown Prophesy Formula, chosen because it "accommodates dichotomous (e.g., right -wrong) answers", yielding a reliability index of 0.68. It was administered to Senior School II students in a non-participating school for validation, and served as both pretest covariate and posttest dependent measure in the ANCOVA.
requirements: Validated via split-half reliability using the Spearman-Brown Prophesy Formula
constraints: Reliability of 0.68 is the value printed for this administration
target_learners: Senior School II students in Nigerian secondary schools
target_learning_goals: civic education literacy
examples: Administered once before the study for validation, then as pretest and posttest in the two intact classes

article_title: Graspable Multimedia: A Study of the Effect of A Multimedia System Embodied with Physical Artefacts on Working Memory Capacity of Preschoolers
citation: Kien Tsong Chau, Zarina Samsudin, Wan Ahmad Jaafar Wan Yahaya. (2018). Graspable Multimedia: A Study of the Effect of a Multimedia System Embodied with Physical Artefacts on Working Memory Capacity of Preschoolers. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Children's Embedded Figure Test (CEFT) as the cognitive-style moderator measure
description: The CEFT is a paper-and-pencil test "designed to determine cognitive style of a subject in the dimension of field-dependence or field-independence," normed for five to twelve year olds. Subjects locate an equilateral triangle and house shapes embedded within 25 larger pictures in 30 minutes, after a ten-minute practice trial, yielding quantitative scores from 0 to 25; scores of 0-11 indicate field-dependence and 12-25 field-independence. In this study it served as the moderator variable classifying the 248 preschoolers.
requirements: 30 minutes testing time plus a ten-minute practice trial; paper-based administration
constraints: Reliability reported from prior sources, ranging from 0.72 to 0.90, with 0.84 to 0.90 for ages 5 to 12
target_learning_goals: cognitive style classification (field-dependence/field-independence)
examples: In Malaysia, a high reliability of 0.87 was reported in a prior research study cited by the authors

article_title: Number Line Estimation with Negatives
citation: Bofferding, L., Hoffman, A., Suazo, E., & Lisy, N. (2015). Number Line Estimation with Negatives. Proceedings of the 37th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. https://www.pmena.org/
title: Case's Central Conceptual Structure for Number and the mental number line
description: The article's theoretical framework draws on Case's (1996) theory of Central Conceptual Structure for Number, in which children first have separate structures for counting objects and visually comparing sets, and around kindergarten begin to coordinate them, mapping numerals to quantities and number words. By first grade, with supportive numerical experiences, these structures are often fully integrated into what the article calls a "mental number line." Extending this structure to negative integers requires accepting numbers less than zero and learning the negative sign's notation, number names, ordering, and values. The study uses this framework to motivate the question of whether integer understanding requires a prior whole-number mental number line.
requirements: Children need supportive numerical experiences for the structures to integrate by first grade
constraints: The article treats the framework as a lens, not as directly tested by the study
target_learning_goals: understanding integer order and values
developing a mental number line including negatives
examples: The study tested whether the board-game intervention would help children extend their mental number line below zero

citation: Balci, C. & Yenice, N. (2016). Effects of the scientific argumentation based learning process on teaching the unit of cell division and inheritance to eighth grade students. Journal of Education in Science, Environment and Health (JESEH), 2(1), 67-84. https://www.jeseh.net
title: Achievement test for the unit of cell division and inheritance (30 items, KR-20 = .86).
description: An achievement test developed by the author to determine students' current knowledge about the cell division and inheritance unit. It initially included 60 items developed based on the stated goals for the unit; following a pilot study and item analysis the number of items became thirty. The analysis showed that its KR-20 reliability coefficient was .86.
requirements: Item analysis following pilot study to select final items
constraints: Specific to the unit of cell division and inheritance in the eighth-grade science and technology course
target_learning_goals: cell division and inheritance content knowledge
examples: Used as pre- and post-test for both experiment and control groups

article_title: A Large Language Model-Powered Multiagent Framework Emulating Standardized Patients in Clinical Communication Skills Training: Development and Evaluation Study.
citation: Qu Yufei, Xu Xiaowei, Long Yunzi, Wang Yijie, Li Jiao, Lu Xudong. (2026). A Large Language Model–Powered Multiagent Framework Emulating Standardized Patients in Clinical Communication Skills Training: Development and Evaluation Study. title: Cerebral cortex–inspired multiagent framework with 5 specialized subagents for SP simulation
description: The article proposes a cerebral cortex–inspired multiagent system (MAS) framework designed to simulate standardized patient (SP) clinical training behaviors. It maps 5 specialized subagents to brain-region functions: a character mapping agent for role traits and motivational states, a memory management agent for contextual encoding and retrieval, an information processing agent for query interpretation, a language generation agent for coherent responses, and a rethinking agent for performance monitoring and error detection. The framework operates in 3 stages—patient construction, diagnostic reasoning, and response generation—and incorporates persistent memory mechanisms to ensure dialogue coherence across conversational turns.
requirements: Requires an LLM core for all subagents to perform tasks such as retrieval, generation, and reflection
Requires clinical case reports as input, along with natural language queries from users and instructional requirements from medical teachers
constraints: The reasoning mode of Qwen3-32B was disabled due to excessive response latency averaging more than 18 seconds, which is unacceptable for practical application
target_learning_goals: clinical communication skills training
medical history taking

title: Three-theme taxonomy of optimal CEP teaching: in situ learning, programme design, and teaching approach
description: The study's thematic analysis generated an organising taxonomy of teaching methods across UK CEP postgraduate degrees. As printed: "Three themes: (1) in situ learning/real-world practice (working with patients and specialist practitioners); (2) programme design (scaffold learning and integrated modules) and (3) teaching approach (simulated learning and research competency) were generated concerning teaching methods and approaches across CEP postgraduate degrees." Each theme carries subthemes supported by verbatim stakeholder quotes in Table 3. A parallel assessment axis yielded two themes: placement tariffs/assessors in situ and role play/simulation.
requirements: Data from semistructured student interviews and academic/CEP focus groups analysed thematically with data saturation reached
constraints: Findings derive from one UK accredited master's course for student participants; generalisability of student insight is limited
target_learners: Postgraduate clinical exercise physiology master's students
target_learning_goals: Clinical skills in exercise risk stratification, testing, prescription, monitoring and outcome assessment
examples: Table 3 pairs each theme with illustrative quotes, e.g. "Patient access in a live setting allows for authentic problem-based learning to take place."

article_title: Middle school students' mental unwellness and academic performance in China: The effects of parental involvement.
citation: Liu Keqiao. (2023). Middle school students’ mental unwellness and academic performance in China: The effects of parental involvement. PLoS One 18(11): e0294172. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0294172
title: China Education Panel Survey (CEPS) longitudinal dataset
description: The China Education Panel Survey is "a nationally representative longitudinal dataset collected by the National Survey Research Center at Renmin University of China", with two publicly available waves. Grade 7 students (Wave 1 N = 10,279) were followed up in Wave 2 (N = 9,449) across 112 schools. It supplied mental unwellness items, parental involvement items, and mid-term test scores used in this study; the minimal replication dataset is posted on the Open Science Framework.
requirements: Panel weight (w1w2sweight) to adjust for student attrition between waves
constraints: No school-level weights provided; mental unwellness measured with the CEPS’s own five-item scale rather than established scales such as GAD-7 or PHQ-9
target_learning_goals: Academic performance in Chinese, mathematics, and English
examples: This study analyzed the Grade 7 cohort followed to Grade 8 with listwise deletion and the w1w2sweight panel weight, yielding a level-1 sample of 7,924 students
